Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a “tool‑centric” recipe for turning your *“I want a burger and fries”* wish into a real McDonald’s order, assuming you only have two black‑box helpers at your disposal: | Step | What you do | Why it matters | |------|-------------|----------------| | **1. Find the right API** | Call the *search* tool with a query such as `"McDonald's online ordering API"` or `"McDonald's mobile app backend endpoints"`. | You need to discover whether McDonald’s exposes a public API, or if you’ll have to go through a third‑party (e.g., Uber Eats, DoorDash). | | **2. Inspect the search results** | Parse the returned URLs and snippets. Look for official documentation, GitHub repos, or developer portals. | Official docs give you the exact endpoints, auth flow, rate limits, and payload schemas. | | **3. Pick an endpoint** | From the docs, locate the “place order” endpoint – often something like `POST /v1/orders` or `POST /api/order`. | That’s where you’ll actually submit the burger + fries. | | **4. Gather prerequisites** | Identify what the endpoint requires:
• Location (lat/lon or zip code)
• Menu item IDs (burger, fries)
• Quantity
• Payment token or card info
• Auth token (OAuth, API key, JWT) | Without these you can’t hit the endpoint successfully. | | **5. Authenticate** | If the API uses OAuth, run the *execute* tool against the auth endpoint (`POST /oauth/token`) with your client credentials to obtain an access token. Store the token for later calls. | Most modern APIs require a bearer token. | | **6. Build the request payload** | Construct a JSON object that matches the schema. Example:
```json\n{\n \"location\": {\"latitude\": 40.7128, \"longitude\": -74.0060},\n \"items\": [\n {\"item_id\": \"BURGER123\", \"quantity\": 1},\n {\"item_id\": \"FRIES456\", \"quantity\": 1}\n ],\n \"payment_method\": \"card_abc123\",\n \"delivery_instructions\": \"Ring the bell\"\n}\n```\n| The payload tells the API exactly what you’re ordering and how to pay. | | **7. Execute the order** | Call the *execute* tool with the full request string:
`POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders`
Headers: `{Authorization: Bearer , Content-Type: application/json}`
Body: the JSON payload from step 6. | This is the actual “order” action. | | **8. Handle the response** | The API will return a status code and a JSON body. Typical fields: `order_id`, `estimated_time`, `status`. Check for `200 OK` or `201 Created`. | Confirm that the order was accepted and capture the order ID for tracking. | | **9. Verify & track** | Optionally, poll a “get order status” endpoint (`GET /v1/orders/`) until the status changes to “delivered” or “completed”. | Gives you real‑time updates on the order. | | **10. Error handling** | If you receive errors (400, 401, 403, 500), log them, retry if transient, or fall back to a different provider (e.g., DoorDash). | Robustness ensures you don’t lose the order due to hiccups. | ### Quick Pseudo‑Code Sketch ```python # 1. Search for the API search_results = search_tool("McDonald's online ordering API") docs_url = pick_best_doc(search_results) # 2. Get auth token auth_resp = execute_tool( url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/oauth/token", headers={"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"}, params={"grant_type": "client_credentials", "client_id": "...", "client_secret": "..."} ) token = auth_resp["access_token"] # 3. Place the order order_payload = { "location": {"latitude": 40.7128, "longitude": -74.0060}, "items": [ {"item_id": "BURGER123", "quantity": 1}, {"item_id": "FRIES456", "quantity": 1} ], "payment_method": "card_abc123" } order_resp = execute_tool( url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}, params=order_payload ) print(order_resp) # Should contain order_id, estimated_time, etc. ``` --- #### Things to Watch Out For | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|------------| | **No public API** | Use a delivery partner’s API (Uber Eats, DoorDash) instead. | | **Item IDs unknown** | Scrape the menu endpoint (`GET /v1/menu`) or use a static mapping table. | | **Payment integration** | Some APIs accept a pre‑generated payment token; others may require you to pass raw card data (PCI‑compliant). | | **Rate limits** | Respect `Retry-After` headers; implement exponential backoff. | | **Location accuracy** | Use GPS coordinates or ZIP codes; some APIs reject orders outside their delivery radius. | By systematically searching for the correct API, authenticating, building the proper payload, executing the call, and handling the response, you can automate the entire “burger + fries” ordering workflow with just the two tools you mentioned.
